title: Slow reading
hookLine: a few lines, read three times, then silence: an old way of reading in many traditions
tomorrow: what's the very first thing the Dhammapada says?

lines: WHAT IT SAYS. ONE WORD. STAYING.
A PAGE CAN DO IT TOO.
cards: A short note from someone who matters often gets read more than once. The first time, for what it says. The second time, slower, one word stands out.

By the third, the reading has turned into something else: staying with it. So, yesterday's question: why would anyone read the same three lines three times? Augustine tells his own story about what a few lines can do.

teach.b: In his Confessions, Augustine sits in a garden in Milan, weeping, stuck between the life he has and the one he wants. From a house nearby he hears a child's voice chanting, "Take up and read; Take up and read."
He picks up the apostle Paul's letters, reads the first passage his eyes fall on, a few lines, and stops. In his words: "No further would I read; nor needed I." A few lines were enough.
Christian monks kept a practice of reading like that and called it lectio divina, holy reading. The Rule of Saint Benedict sets hours of the monk's day aside for it.

teach.h: A LADDER: READ, CHEW, TASTE, REST.
teach.b: A Carthusian monk named Guigo drew it as a ladder with four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation. His picture is a meal. Reading puts the food in your mouth.
Meditation chews it. Prayer tastes it. Contemplation is the sweetness itself.
Some groups who practice it today read one short passage aloud three times, with silence after each. The first reading is for what it says. The second is for one word or phrase that stands out.
The third is for staying with that word. Then the reading stops, and the quiet does the rest. A guest at that table can borrow the pace without claiming the prayer.

how: In some lectio divina groups today, one person reads a short passage aloud three times, with silence after each reading, and the others listen for a word or phrase that stands out.

games.q: your neighbor reads the same small prayer card every morning. your friend says she must be bored of it by now. what does a slow reader say?
o: maybe the opposite: a few lines, read again and again, keep opening.
probably. she'd get more from a new reading every morning instead.
it's just a habit; after so long the words don't really count.
games.why: slow reading goes back to the same lines on purpose. read three times, a passage shows something new each time.

practice: Here are two verses of Psalm 23, read as a guest.

Read them aloud, slowly, three times, with a breath of silence after each: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters."
Any three lines you love will do instead. Then set the words down and stay in the quiet for whatever time is left.

wordCard.voice: Slow reading: a few lines, read three times, then silence. The monks' name for it was lectio divina.

orig.note: Latin: holy reading, the monks' slow way with scripture. Guigo's four rungs are lectio, meditatio, oratio, contemplatio.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: three times, then quiet. Two days in, and the books are open.
